blocks.x: I forgot certain incidents at places like we played in London before we came back to America. We were asked by the British government to play at the Savoy Hotel. That was a celebration of the Peace Victory Ball. Yeah we worked to play the dance music and we went on over there after they had all the parades and all kinds of ceremonies in the street all day. People were kissing one another. Men were even kissing you on the street. They were so happy. That night we went over to the Savoy Hotel and we mounted the stand. They had 50 piece band in the United States Marine Band and probably about the same in the English band. And they're both bands got up and played the Star Spangled Banner and God Save the King. Now we were pointed out to get up and start the dance program. Instead of that just a handful of musicians got up and played the Star Spangled Banner. And when we played that number and finished it with just three blowing instruments, a piano and drums. Those people were amazed at the amount of music that could come out in a few horns. The house came down. In the Orleans was the King and Queen of England, the King of Belgium, General Pushin and his staff, General Pushin and many notables of Europe. And when we played after the Star Spangled Banner and the applause subsided, we went into the Tiger Rag which would be the first number. And when them people got up and danced, you didn't know what you were looking at. It was just a dazzle of jewelry. They had tiaras on them. They had all kinds of beautiful clothes, which I have never seen before. And the uniforms of the men just sparkled with all kinds of brass epaulets and different things like that. We looked like we was in a land of some story that I had when I was a child. Great things. We looked around there and even the King applauded. All of them applauded for us. We went into the second number and we never did stop playing one number after the other until the ball was over. We were the greatest hit there. That finished that night. When the NC4 was flown over with Commander Reed, they had a private reception for him. Again, the English government called on us to play for them. And at Marble Arch, we entertained Commander Reed and the English nobility again there. That was at Marble Arch. That was when the NC4 flew from America to England. I don't know which port they came from, but I have in these clippings of mine, autographs of Commander Reed. Now those are the two things that I forgot. Now when we came back to America, we got taking Edwards back in the band and I was to take Christian and have him play bass violin because he had known a little bit about it. About bass violin, all of us piddled around, all the speakers. We always piddle around different instruments. Like I used to play guitar sometimes, I'd try to play bass. I didn't play bass good, but nobody would know it because when I started slapping on the bass, there ain't nothing but a sound but a slap. A tempo would come out of it. So Amy would play bass. He may have played better than me, but he would have filled in until he learned. But he wanted to go back to England. He had other things that he wanted to tent over there. So I bought Amy or Cher out so he could get enough money to go back to England. What I mean by Cher, when we played royalties for Concerns, we got an artist royalty. The same as like Caruso would get. Now I don't mean the two cents that you get for the copy, which two cents went to the publisher and one cent come to us. We got 50%. We got two cents royalty plus money for setting. For instance, a nominal fee which would pay around $150 for the date. Plus a two cents royalty on every record that would be sold. Well I bought his Cher out so he managed him to go back to England. Well when he got back there was around September or so I couldn't exactly tell you the date. He asked to form a band over there for Mr. Mitchell who the man I had just left that wanted to sign us to another year contract before we left England. I didn't want to stay in England no more. I had various reasons that I can't tell why I had to leave England. I wouldn't want to tell but maybe someday someone may find out but right now I wouldn't tell. We came back to New York. Amy went back to London and he asked me to get him some money. At this time they had many New Orleans musicians that was out of work in New York. I wanted to send him New York men. He didn't want New York men. He wanted Philly Napoleon and Johnny Costello and men that knew the Dixieland style of music. I have his letter here. If someone would care to read into it which if I read it they'll say that I'm telling none of the truth. Will you stop the machine? Sure. Love New York men. I may have made a mistake. I've been corrected by my brother. Emil did not want New Orleans men. He wanted men from New York who knew the Dixieland style and the numbers. I hope you'll be able to erase that first part if I did make that mistake off. But I'll have someone to read that letter in there. So when you hear this man speak he may speak different today because everybody wants to claim as creators. You want to look at?

Yes that's right. We'll keep it now. This is a letter from Emil Christian and it says I would like Philip Napoleon on cornet and Johnny Costello on clarinet. The boys I was working with because they have more of an idea what I want and they can play all the Dixieland numbers because I'll know we'll get some requests for them. It's signed on the back here. Sincerely, Emil Christian, 2 Bagley Street, Tidingham Court Road, Apartment 1, London, England. And I don't see the date. Let me think. It's on the 1st. The date is September 6, 1920.

Now from this letter you'll see this is a New Orleans man. I could have had him shopping. I could have got him Gardena, Giardina, Tony Giardina was around New York doing nothing. And I had contacted these men finally. But he wanted men who copied from the Dixieland records. We'll go to show you that even the New Orleans boys didn't want the boys from New Orleans because they didn't know the rhythm. That is the truth that I am sitting here and telling you that no New Orleans band played the rhythm that was contained in the original Dixieland jazz band recording. They had to acquire it by listening to it. Well the New Orleans boys were setting away of their own. They couldn't see and they couldn't feel. The same as the Negroes that came. They thought they had the rhythm. They were making ta-ta-ta-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Well that is an ending I make on many of my pieces played eight years before them. Ta-ta-ta-da-da-da-da-da-da. Tip된 stuff with a saxophone. They forced us to use a saxophone because throughout the country there was something about eliminating jazz because it was ruining the morals of the girls. Well we made these records, they sold, sold into millions but they were not the same as the other record. You take a man playing from the north who had not copied the style although he was a technical man. There was no better saxophone player than him yet he couldn't fit in the band properly. It broke up a sort of the rhythm of the band. A lot of people says the demise of the original Dixieland Jan was dead. No, we were forced to the wall by laws. John Rhodes Stratton went to Albany, New York in 1921 and passed laws prohibiting jazz bands from playing on Broadway. We were the only jazz band playing on Broadway. We had to give up the contract with the Father of the Bajer because we were the player the fall and winter. That was when they put Gildegary in jail for doing the shimmy. And they stopped the band at 12 o'clock.

I hate to interrupt you on that story but I missed out a couple of things. I didn't get who was in the band at the time. I know Edwards was back. He replaced Christian and I didn't get the names of the other bands.

Now I'll tell you the names of the men. Robertson joined us as piano player which he had been the first steady piano player after Regis' death. We had Shields, myself, Spobara, Edwards and what's his name? Roberts had made the five of us.
And that's immediately upon coming back from London. That's right. Robertson Hilton. And then what was the name of the saxophone players? I want to get that to you.
It was Benny Kruger. Benny Kruger. One of the most versatile men in New York at the time. Yes sir. But he was not a jazz man.
So now back to Gilda Gray and her shimmy.

Well Gilda Gray did the shimmy and I think she stayed there about maybe two weeks. They put her in there as a sort of showcase so she could get a job in one of the big shows. Well I'll tell you who Gilda Gray was. It was the wife of Gil Bogue. Gil Bogue, Jimmy Thompson and Mr. Salvin owned this Follies Bragé at the top of the Winter Garden. They were the owners of it. Sam Salvin operated as a manager of it. But these other men were the partners. And they only brought Gilda Gray in there to do that dance with us for a showcase. And right after that she got a big part of the Zip Field Follies.
Now what did people object to in the dance?

Well they said we had a sexual music that we were ruining the morals of the girls. They, people would get out there and they'd forget they were dancing, standing in one spot and starting moving around. In other words the great masters tried to move them. But they didn't succeed. I guess ours was like wine or good wine. When the people would get interested in our music. They'd stand there. Some of them would dance around. Stand there and they just moved themselves like worms. And many of the times we'd sneak off to a bandstand. We'd play low. Very low. Very low. And one by one we'd sneak off the bandstand. There was nobody on the stand. These people with their feet were keeping the rhythm. Perfect rhythm on, on you know with the scraping of their feet on the floor. All of a sudden someone would look at the bandstand. There'd be nobody there and you'd talk about a howl. Well to begin. Let me tell you about a certain psychology I used to use. Of course I'm stupid. But I know it takes one monkey to start clapping and hollering and the rest will follow. In my home I had a way that I could imitate a woman's voice. Holler. Whoooo. Just like that. And nobody knew where it would come. It would come out the horn and look like it was a hundred feet away. Before they'd know where it was coming from. Mr. Schultz many times would put people out and they didn't do a thing. It was that hollering. I'd get them so they would be in ecstasy. They wouldn't know where they'd be hollering and stomping more and more and more. And they'd be dropping ten, twenty, and fifty dollar bills in the sugar can. And the more I'd hollered they wouldn't leave the floor. They'd have to take us off the bandstand and get us away so the people could go buy refreshments. That was both at Rice Webbers and this place. 1922 we were relegated to a dance hall. We went to work at Healy's. It was turning into a dance hall for 60 of us only. I worked there about five weeks. Wait, I had my story. Before we went to the dance place, I went on a series of one night stands. stuff

many of the places we had returning engagements. Through my files, you'll be able to see the office of jobs we had. And all the New Orleans boys was not working. And if I'd have had a thousand men that could play our music, I could have been a millionaire today because I had jobs for all of them. But there was none of them could fit the bill. In this one-night stands, we came back. And it was a tough job, riding all night to go to another place. For instance, you'd jump from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh. It was almost a whole 12-hour ride. Pennsylvania's a big state. It ain't like New Orleans or Baton Rouge. You can make it in a couple hours. But over there, you took a train. If you went by car, it would take you all day long. Maybe a day and a half to get there. So we used to go in on an $850 or $750 guarantee, plus 50% of the takeover over $800 some odd. I'd had a man stationed at the door with one of these little meters. The admission was $1.10 for ladies and women. When they went in there, each time one passed through the door, this man would click this little machine what he had in his pocket. The man in the office didn't know that we were keeping tab. At 11 o'clock, I'd come down and find out how much money we had. I wasn't worried about who coming after 11 o'clock. All I was worried about getting what I had coming to me at that time. And I didn't care if they let him in free after that. So we played in places like armrests. Some of these rubber-lipped men without electrical equipment, they couldn't be hooded. 50 feet. You had to have power and lungs made of steel to fill a place almost a half a square long and a square wide. Or a square long and a half a square wide. Either way you put it. And as many as 5,000 to 8,000 to 10,000 people would be in there jammed in there. They had alternate bands. They had 8,000, 10,000, 12 pieces would play on the opposite side of us. And when we played, everybody got to dance. When they played, nobody danced. Sometimes our shift would go for half an hour as long as they'd applaud. I'd stare there pouring at them because we wanted to come back. 11 o'clock, I'd go pick up this money like I told them. Check up with the men. Some men were honest. Some would try to cheat me. Well, I didn't mind if they beat me out of $100 because they had a little extra expense. We had nothing to put out. Just come there dry with our instruments. No music to carry. No sound equipment. No one to pay this man. If it was a question of $100, $150, I wouldn't open my mouth. When it comes to about $400 or $500, I'd squawk for my end of it. I'd take $400. I'd shove it in my pocket. I'd take the rest of it, whether it's $1,200 or $1,800. I had a money belt made that fit around my waist. And I'd take this money and shove it in my belt all around like that. None of the boys would walk with me. They're afraid that someone might hold me up and kill me. They'd run off. Some of them would stand around watching. But I had to go get a cab and ride to a hotel and hold that money in my possession all night until the bank opened the next morning that these boys could get money on us and send them to wherever they wanted to send them. This money was split five ways. I never got a dime extra outside of expenses like telegraphs. A different thing. It was a cooperating band. And everything I did was cooperative. Today, the boys said they kept books for me. But it's untrue. Because they're going to look through these papers and find out that they got the best break. I didn't get the best break. I did the work. I did the brain work. I composed all the numbers. I did everything in the band. I knew it was my only opportunity in life to make a success. I'm working for my boy. Fifteen years old. You'll know what it is when you see something in front of you that you can make money out of it. You're not going to let that opportunity pass you. And that was my motto. Opportunity to knock once. We came back to New York. We was tired. I went to wait and sign a contract for Sixty Bazzoni. I think that's S-I-X-T-I. He was a man that run a lot of dance schools. He must have been about eight or nine dancing ballaces around New York. I'm going to enter my story. After we finished his one night, Shields had given his notice that he intended to retire from the music dance. I had already changed the piano. I forgot to tell you that too. At the Follies Bouget. When Robertson failed to come through with his agreement, he was to give us a thousand dollars for the band for plugging Margie and making Margie a hit song. Up to this time, Robertson never had a hit. I'm all mixed up on this thing, but if you listen, you get these things, you'll be able to get them right. Right. And I plugged Margie and singing the blues and many other Robertson's numbers. And I was instrumental in getting this thing to be recorded by Victor in 1920. When Robertson got his first statement, they had sold about a million and a half records. He must have got about eight, nine thousand dollars of money for himself. There were three men interested in that. There were three of them who used to pay this money. And they reneged on it, a thousand dollars. That was... I can't think of the other man's name, but the names are on the song. You will see. Robertson was in the band. And now I gave Robertson his two weeks notice and replaced him with Frank Signorelli. At this time, Frank Signorelli and Johnny Costs and them had a little band. They called them Memphis Five. They were copies of what they copied off the original Big Slayer Jazz Band recordings and stuff. And this boy had not much time, but only go over a few little other numbers that he didn't know our arrangements on. In the afternoon, I got to play them openly, showing them different parts of where to make the break and all. And each night, we had a different number at all so it wouldn't be too hard for him to remember. And that was the band that we went to Atlantic City before we went on the one night stands. I tell you that too. It was here that they went with Sophie Tucker too. It was Bill Lewis, Sophie Tucker. Our building was in lights on the outside of the building. It remained there for a year after that we weren't playing there. There was Katz's place. I don't remember the name now, but if you look up my pieces of paper that's in there, you'll find the contract of Katz, the amount of money we got from him. And we got room and board with this contract that was agreed that we were to get room and board. Then we went on the one night stand. It was this time that Shields was getting too hard. Shields had already married before we went to London and his wife couldn't travel with him and he was away from his wife. And from this money he was making, almost $1,000 a week for about eight, nine weeks, he thought he was fat. This money would last him forever. I don't know where he went, whether he went to Chicago or California. I wouldn't know because I never corresponded with him. He didn't correspond with me. Now we go to the balconies, Jimmy Light Town, which played with Signorella in the Memphis Five when the first of all was a young boss in Brooklyn joined my band. After five weeks, I went down with Influenza. I pulled the band out rather than put substitutes in there. When I pulled the band out, that's when they formed the Memphis Five and brought them into the balconies. This is the beginning of the notoriety of the Memphis Five. He had learned the numbers and the arrangements by playing along with the original Dix-Solene Jazz Band, which I had taught this, Signorella, and Light Town. It was easy for them to have Mick Moore and her drummer sit in and play with them because that was the nucleus of their band. They had the two men right there. All they needed was the trombone and the drums to fill out their band. They made many records for Sam Lanham on the last Black Aces. Some of the arrangements they'd taken that Frank Signorelli won especially, and I wish I could shimmy like my sister Kate. Almond P. Ron in 1917 sent me this music and asked me if I could set this music for recording. I had never known P. Ron but I heard him play. He used to play most of all the white society dances. He and Robe Show, they had all the society dances. Very few white bands ever played for society. Always these two Negro bands. Now they played conventional ragtime music. The music of that era which was played by white men also.
Were they raiding?

Raiding, there were no raiding. Absolutely no greeners. Were they fake at all? I don't know. I wasn't allowed in the place. Oh, I see. The how come, I used to be an electrician in my early days. And many times I was sent to DeSoto Hotel to do work over underneath there. You know, they were on electrical equipment. Or some line would go out and I'd have to pull new wires through it. I worked for Mark's construction company at that time. That was down in 531 Island Institute. That was the biggest, largest electrical construction in the South. These people wired at places like Monroe, electrical power places. all through the Louisiana. Zimmerman Lumber Company run an auxiliary line from Zimmerman, Louisiana into Monroe, which is about 10, 15 miles. I climbed every pole in there, put every high power line that was ever put in Monroe in the beginning. I worked on all that. and that's how I used to hear the colored band because whenever I went down there and they had some functioning in the De Soto Hotelers, most of all they used to give them, I could hear them playing.
Did Robichaux's band and Huron's band have a hot tone? Would you say they had a jazz tone or a legitimate tone or what?

Well, I'd say they played the same, I think they recorded I have never heard their records but for enough people I've heard they didn't have jazz. Now I'm not quoting myself because what I heard, I heard the same music in white bands. They mention many bands but they don't mention Bowers, the Christians, the Detroit's band and the Cordy's band. They don't mention none of the white bands, all the Negroes as a culture Louisiana music. That's not right. Because the culture of Louisiana music, it was because of so many parades, so many affairs that was given. Let me start in the beginning, I told you about the string bands that I played in and let me tell you some of the places where I went. On July the 4th, they celebrated, that was American Day. July the 14th was Bastille Day, some places, Southern Park, sometimes other places that different great big places that did these affairs. That'll last sometimes two days. Then they had the Volksfest which was German. They had three, four bands that have a whole German band there and plenty of other bands that they don't mention. There's none of this stuff here that they have here. They had men like Sontagy played in the French opera, Pippa Tony. Some men that, these Negroes and I then, many modern men couldn't even touch. They were men that come from the conservatory that learned their music away from here. They had Germans. There's one old man here who used to play at a college restaurant, Shutton. Mr. Shutton, he used to bomb down the alley too. I used to go as a young boy.
You know, he didn't mention none of these men

but Negroes. But they don't tell you what they played. They say what they played. But they don't have no proof. No white men played music. In the French opera, they'll tell you the Italians didn't have nothing. Most of it was Italian opera and Italian singers. There had other plays there. You're going to ask me why? I worked on the French opera stage. As a boy, I attended two arc lights on there. And many of the ideas I got from them. Listen to the songs that they used to play. Like playing counter melody. Two songs line at one time.

which became counterpoint in my case. If you listen to Livestable Blues, you'll see what I mean. Take each instrument alone and you've got three melodies in there. That's what old timers call a fugue. We didn't know what to call it. We didn't call it anything until they named it for us in Chicago. We didn't know what it was. We played it. That's all. Now, there was a sound. The father of this Detroit, Johnny Detroit's father had a band, a very good band. There was Mr. Bowler who had a band. Mr. who? Bowler. B-O-H-L-E-R. There was this fellow. I don't mean shoving them. They had ragtime bands. There was Johnny Shimmer.
Shimmer Manor had a band. Who? Shimmer Manor.

Yeah. Or Shimmer Manor. Shimmer Manor's band. They were all playing by notes. And they played in the carnival parades. Jack Lane played in the carnival parades. He hired some men who played by music. And he had some fakers in his band. And he also had some men who didn't play at all. Which they were called potato men. When you ask Jack Lane, when you go there, ask him about the potato men. How he made his money on unfortunate men. He had seven men playing. He played a bass drum. I'd be built and blowing my guts out on the carnival. And he had his son with a potato and an alto horn blowing to the ground blowing the dust off the floor. No music was coming out. He got paid for the parade. Then he'd have one or two other boys that was hangers on. There'd be seven men playing. There should have been ten playing. That's the kind of music he put out. He didn't look for music. He didn't know music. He wasn't even a musician. Yet, this man has believed in many things. That is the kind of people they give cupster at the jazz club. Then they had Tom Brown's band. It was a ragtime band. These boys went to Chicago before I did. I want to tell the truth about everything because if I tell you that I went before them, someone else before. But before these boys left, New Orleans was like a clearing house. And they had many men that was recruited out of the alley. That went in. You want me to go back to Pierron and AJ Pierron and Shaving Like My Sister Kate? Mm-hmm. And what happened there? Well, let me tell you the beginning then because I'm repeating some of this stuff. When we were at Rising Web and we were the big hit, Pierron sent to me a bundle of music to try to play for me. This is before Williams had joined his family. And amongst them was Sister Kate and I wish I could shimmy like my, no, I wish Mama's Baby Boy and Brown Skin Who You For, which they laid a place and with Will Ross of Chicago. This arrangement that we made on Sister Kate became famous around New York. Everybody wanted Sister Kate because it was a good number for them to play and fit in good jazz. Now you asked me about what kind of music Pierron played. Well, he played the same as any other band that played from notes. I see no difference in the music that he played and what white men, that is white men were playing at the time. They were Robichaud's band. They played too. Now whether they played by fake or by notes, I cannot attest to that because I was not in the room. But to me, it didn't sound any different than the music that I heard white men play at the different dances that were given at the different picnic grounds and other places of their era.
Now, what about Lytel and Signorelli and their recording of Sister Kate?

They took the whole arrangement in total and recorded it. That's what they did. And they made Sister Kate. Now I had correspondence with A.J. Perron. I just can't find it at present. I would like to include that in there to show you that Perron and I correspond before Francis Williams ever came to New York.
Before who was this came to be?

I mean Clarence Williams. You got me right that time because I'm making a mistake. I'm just telling you, I'm reading. I'm not reading. I'm telling you from my mind. Clarence Williams came to New York around 1923. The first white man he met on Broadway was me with an introduction from A.J. Perron, which you'll find in their books too. And this Negro is supposed to have her buddy bowling play. Now let me tell you about this man, who he is, where he come from. If any of you serious scholars doubt me, I was just speaking about Clarence Williams when he came to New York. Now if any of you serious scholars doubt what I say, you look up the history of Clarence Williams. He was supposed to have heard Buddy Bowling play. Buddy Bowling, according to the statistics given out by the New Orleans Jazz Club, was incarcerated in the Crazy House. That's Jackson, Louisiana. In 1906. He was put in jail and held there a year before they put him in the Crazy House. That was 1906. This would make Clarence Williams about six years old or seven. Because at the age of eight years old, he lived with his grandmother in an alley in Plaquemine, Louisiana, where he was a shoeshine boy from a gentleman by the name of Ferdinand, H-E-R-B-E-R-T, Herbert, who ran a barber shop in the city of Plaquemine. Now this Negro didn't come to New Orleans to his late teens. He could have never heard Buddy Bowling play. This same thing applies to Little Louie. Little Louie heard the records of the original Dixieland Jazz Band, but I can tell you he never heard Bowling play. Stop the machine on me. Wait now. Little Louie, the man I'm talking about is Louis Armstrong, who's style is playing off the ostrich walk. If you serious scholars get down and listen to his record, Sweet Little Papa or Little Pa, you'll see what Little Rock is talking about. I want you to read a letter from Mr. Fowler. Just that paragraph where it comes in and talks about Louie's young life in New Orleans.

All right. This is a letter dated May the 27th, 1958 from Don Fowler, 9441 Southwest 8th Drive, Portland 1, Oregon. It's to D. James, D. James, Nick LaRocca, at 2218 Constant Street, New Orleans, 13, Louisiana. And here's a paragraph that Mr. LaRocca would like for me to read. The other day I ran across an interesting statement by Louis Armstrong in his book, Satchmo. He is discussing his life in New Orleans in 1918, and this is a paragraph. Quote, One day when it was raining like mad, Daisy and I went in the front room listening to some new records I had just bought. New releases of the original Dixieland jazz band, which we were playing on an upright victroler we were proud of. The records were Livery Stable Blues and Tiger Rag, the first Tiger Rag to be recorded. Paren, between you and me, it's still the best. Paren, unquote.
Now read down where he says the other steel in the music of the Dixieland band, Louisiana Five.

I have a record of Virginia Blues by the Louisiana Five in which they play the third strain of Skeleton Jangle as a part of the tune. It's signed, uh, Sincerely Yours, Don Fowler. Is there anything else you want to read?

You know, that's all. Not only the Louisiana Five, but everybody. It was a field lead from the all steel music and different things out the original Dixieland jazz band. Now they say these Negroes didn't hear these records. Joe heard them. If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them. Because Joe, in his thing, that's what he bases his rhythm on. Because he didn't know no better. He was just a Negro that didn't know no better. Like these even white crumbs who's supposed to be historians around New Orleans. They can't be honest people. I have a statement in one of the second line about Miss Myra Manfeld. She says, it never rains, but it pours. Marshall Stein is in town with the Guggenheimer Foundation. Well, this ain't a laugh. This is a laugh. She says, whenever they come to find out of jazz, I see that they go see the right people. Now here's a woman, maybe in 40 years of age, interested in herself to be pro-Negro. Marshall Stein, who is a pro-Negro, and is the cause of integration of bands, and is the cause of softening the morals of the integrated people of the South. This man belongs to a society, a young man's Christian Hebrew Association. He has it on his letter. I'd like to read that letter to you, or have someone read it for me. All right. To bring you up to date on this thing, this happened in 1936, when I was to reorganize the band, and this Tom Brown had given a lot of information that was untrue. He said he had the first original Dixieland jazz band, but he didn't make no claims at this time of composing any numbers. That came later. When he got mixed with Sushon, that all came up later, about the numbers that he had composed. But I want you to read that.

The letter here from... Let me see. I'll give you the full letterhead. It's a letter from Marshall W. Stearns. Yale Hot Club, 6th Linwood Place, New Haven, Connecticut. M. W. Stearns, President. Charter Unit of the UHCA. January the 11th, 1937, Mr. D.J. La Rocca, Earl Theater, Washington, D.C. Dear Nick, I have all your records from Liberty Stable Blues to the recent disc. I like the earlier ones better. Between you and me, our last argument should furnish you with plenty of publicity. I do think, however, that you fail to give colored musicians a break. And that is why I exaggerated the other extreme, since the public is inclined to believe you and musicians of your opinion. There is nothing I should like better than to see your scrapbook. However, I am still in school and will be teaching next year. If I ever get the chance, I shall certainly drop in and say hello. Let's keep up the battle. Sincerely, Marshal W. Stearns. That's a signature, and it has M. W. Stearns, President, typed underneath. Its initials are given M. W. Stearns, and M. J. L. as his titus.

From this article, many other articles was copied. This is a work, you've got to be either pro-communist or a communist to work this way. There's a letter to keep me quiet. I'm a working man, trying to support a family. This man has not stopped writing about Negroes, yet he knows different. Now here's Brown's letter. To show you Brown was lying, I want to show you, I want to have him read this in there, what the name of his band was, in case you ever read Downbeat on 1936, and see what they have did to a man who has did nothing to anyone but tried to make a living and be honest in his ways of life. Would you read this letter here?

This is dated New Orleans, Louisiana, 10-21-36. Dear friend Nick, received your letter and was very glad to hear from you. Was glad to hear that you are in good health. as this letter leaves me the same. Was also glad to hear that you are doing good and hope you will continue to do so. If I remember correctly, the building of the band when we were in Chicago playing at the Lambs Cafe was Brown's Band from Dixieland. We opened an engagement there on a short time after May the 15th. Sorry I'm not able to furnish you with any exact dates as all the clippings I had... ... ...

destroyed by fire since returning home we were built at a theater in Hoboken New Jersey as Brown's band Kings of Ragtime that was during the latter part of 1915 I think also played an engagement at the Century Theater in New York and played Lowe's it says Lowe's time as the musical rules give my regards to Larry Tony and any of the other boys I know my wife sends her best regards wishing you the best of luck and success I remain your friend Bill Lambert

that is a drummer of Brown's band now you historians all his turns including the great mr. Sushant go look up and see if you see any building of them but you're willing to print that they were the first original Dixieland jazz band you're not only about to be ashamed of yourself you should go to the top of the new bridge and jump off that's where you belong because if you were around this person as you say you're intelligent you have an education which I have not got but I have more truth in my little finger than you got in your whole body you have lied to the people you have told them truths I'm not suffer by it you will and miss men will go down she deserted to sink and ship after I sent her a few letters that will go down in history if the honor scholar will listen to my letters they'll know what they did to me around New Orleans they're not only persecuted me you mean little of me there's not a man ever lived since the time of Jesus Christ that they put so much lies against for what I never know they say I was trying to take the credit for everything now if you were leader of a band and you were out there before others and you know they didn't play that you wouldn't see Al Jolson say that Eddie Cantor was Al Jolson no that's different but me I'd have to say they did play what I did to say that they did play what I did to say. I played nine oh they're liars I'm not gonna say it because I'm gonna tell the truth they didn't play what I played the fact is it's not only one number that I compose but I have about 20 of them published already and I got at least 30 of them home and I can make another thousand before I die if I want them right now because I know how to compose it too I know how to arrange it they didn't have that they didn't have that and that was the beginning what we did was the beginning of all name bands came special arrangements came all what you want but the Dixieland showed the way original Dixieland. Dixieland I want to come to a part where we played the St. Louis Blues of course this will bring me back into 1920 again but this is the only way I can get it on as I come to these things.
Didn't Mr. Erkwood read that? A letter from Handy is that it?
I believe he did. See that's why. Yeah.
Yeah. Well I think.

I admitted to you that Brown's band went to Chicago before we did. The people didn't notice them any different. They made no success. So I can't see where they introduced anything. They had many bands like I told you before in the Orangewood's Clarence.
I read a better letter where you asked him if you wanted to meet him before the jazz club. Oh yeah. Well I'll get to that. I understand.

And he's got me all mixed up now this guy. That's all right. And see stop it. When Brown went to Chicago the members of his band was not as he gives them in the later part of his band. The band consisted of Billy Lambard drums, Gus Miller clarinet, Raymond Lopez cornet, this fellow Lloyd Canna, Arnold Lloyd Canna, guitar, and Theo Brown bass. It's like Canna says he had taken music by some professor who learned more than one lesson than the kids learned in three years today. Well to tell you the truth I don't want to knock this man but I never heard him play piano outside of chords like I play. Maybe he plays him a little better than me because he has been playing along and more steady than I have played. But I always known him to be a guitar player. That's all I ever seen him play in New Orleans. Now if he played piano in every band he played with he played bass. He may have played in Brown's band piano. Maybe that accounted for their failure. I don't know. But they didn't have the rhythm. Because if they did and they went before us it would have been to their glory and not the original Dixieland jazz band who came after them as they say. Because no one noticed their music. No one noticed their music of being anything different but ragtime as they build themselves. Now I was trying to tell you about New Orleans being a musical town and I was interrupted by my brother. New Orleans was a place when men came here and they wanted to recruit a band. They'd come in the exchange alley and they had men that traveled all over the United States. Maybe Mexico and any place that circuses or road shows would go. This is before Brown ever went to Chicago. Because I happened to be in the alley and know. I spoke to many of the old timers and that like fellas now at Ricky Toms. He had bands that went out to circuses. Traveled all over the United States through Chicago and all. He played ragtime, played like the rest of them played around here by notes, ragtime. But Brown's band was part fake and part readers. Lopez could read and so could Miller read and the rest of them were fakers. Tom Brown was a faker. Now.
So now how did this trombone play as different say from Edwards?

Well, he never played any kind of trombone until years after. You'd have to verify that by the records he supposed to have played with different bands. Edwards was the daddy of all modern trombone players. And nobody could compete with Edwards on the trombone. Although he and I are enemies today. I'll give him what is due. The man was the greatest trombone player of his age. He invented many tricks on the trombone. Which was to be followed by men like Miff Moe. Tea gardens and all of them. Which they improved. Now you say, well why didn't he do this and why didn't he do that? Now let me tell you something. You must have a starting point for everything. We had no records to fashion ourselves behind. They had our records to fashion behind. The only record I ever played was like I told you against the marches, so it was his marches and all. And from the noodles in there I built my own tunes. Well they may say they're no good. Other men have did the same thing. It's not only I did it. The great masters did it. A modern man did it. I've seen tunes like I'm Sorry I Made You Cry and all that. And they'll reverse it and put the chords a little bit different. Use the same chords construction. And who's sorry now? It's the same chords construction. But they're modern and they're not Nick LaRocca. But if Nick LaRocca did that, that would have been wrong. That would have been all wrong. He done took somebody else's tune. But two other different guys that didn't have nothing to do with jazz did it. It's perfectly alright. Now on the chord construction at Tigeray, you can put in that, what you call this? This parade you got there. Bourbon Street Parade, it'll fit it. And Washington Lee Swing or Tulane Swing, whatever you want to call it, it'll fit it. And over the waves will fit it too. So therefore, if they want to get technical, call it all over the waves and give the day a break on Italian. Call it that. If they want to go back to where they want to build up the chord construction, that's where the tune came from. Sombra Solis. That's the right name of it. That's some of the tunes I played in my early days. And that's what they played around here in the early days. They had no American music. Hardly any American music then. Most of the music was imported from away from here. It only started around 1900s. They started. And the first man to put ragtime in music was Scott Joplin. And I think he was from Texas. And many of the tunes that he played, I didn't copy from him. But he had three parts like all the rest of the people of that day. And you'll find most of our tunes had three parts that had a trio to it, which was copied by other people. I copied from someone else, but in a different rhythm. When we played the rhythm of our band, it was entirely different than the rhythm that had preceded us. It was different entirely. Because if it was different, no one would have noticed us. We would have been like Tom Brown or Ricky Tom, anybody else. We would have been just passing through. But wherever we went, we were a success. I know Claire, if we played in a dive, we were a success. We jammed the place. All they had to pass and hear us, and they'd come in. It was something that appealed to them. Today, they don't play jazz the way we play. You'll ask me why? Well, they got a bunch of rubber-lipment men. They're good for one chorus. If I had to play one chorus, maybe I could straighten the bell out. The horn wouldn't have stayed still. It would have stretched straight out. When they play the one chorus, they're finished. Then they come in on the last chorus. They don't play the tune through in unison the same way we did. They play a whole night, some nights. We played as long as 17 hours a night. They couldn't even begin to start. Less than one hour, they'd have laid that horn down like I made Richard Brunis lay his down and beluxed it. This man came over there. He was going to show me up, show me what kind of lip he had. Jack Lane hired him. I had told you about this parade. Came over there before the day was over. He said, let me take the high C. Good, take it, Richie. I know what conserving the lip is. I know when to blow hard and know when to blow easy. I never take the horn from my mouth. Once it's up there, it stays there from the beginning to the end of the tune. I never went in for high notes. But at my command, I could make a high C any day. That is a high B on the piano. It's a high C on the trumpet. I could make it any time. And I could have went above that. But when you're playing alone, after you make your high C and D, what comes after that? Nothing. Not with the original Dixieland Jazz Band. It had to keep moving. And I was always there driving. In the driver's seat, driving that band. Whenever I played, I constructed the thing. Larry put the lace on and Edgwood sewed it up. And there was no band that ever came behind us, ever played like us. I've heard bands try. They've tried to copy these things down notation. Can't be done. You can't play another man's style. It's got to be stiff. Just like Joe thought he had the rhythm. He was stiff. You want to listen to his record, good. And you'll change your mind. If you're a musician, you've got to change your mind. But if you're just pro and you don't care and you're biased in your opinion, well, you stick to your own opinion. That ain't going to hurt me any. But as the people know, are beginning to find out, since they reissued the Victor wouldn't reissue the records, I tried to have them put them out when this controversy came up. But there's different hands that run the Victor today than running the Victor company when I was a young man. But some influence, the Colombian put these records out. And these records are sold all over the world. And they begin to find out. How could these men play so better than these Negroes in the eight, nine years ahead of them? How could they do that if they copied the Negro? How could they do it? How could they do it? How could they do it? I'll leave that to Dr. Shushone and Mr. Meyer Menville to explain to me that rhythm came from Africa. Now, rhythm is not necessarily music. I don't say. But I never heard that rhythm in Africa. The only place I heard it was in the records of the original Dixieland Jazz Band. He heard it in Africa because he read Marshall Stein's book, who was pro-Negro, who was trying to give the Negro culture. I don't say the Negro don't play better today than he played then, but look what he has. He has a school that teaches and many are taught by white men, music. I had nobody to teach me. I taught myself. I'm not here trying to sway anybody to what I tell them, but only a man that couldn't read.

would have to make up such stuff to fake, like brrrr through a horn. And different other little things that he didn't know the tune would add, different little things, which later became known as jazz licks or jazz idioms. It was just like a fake, a bunch of gypsies, didn't know nothing. And not knowing the tune, we'd fall back on it. Now I could tell you, many of the fellows, they put them all together these tunes, these idioms. They'll start do all together. When he finished that one chord construction with that tune, let me see him play another tune behind it. Well I didn't do that. I could have played the same way. But after I finish one tune in that same chord construction, they were all alike, they became all alike. There was no difference. So I was a limited man. I limited my licks. I limited the different little things that I could put into it, saving it for somewhere else for a little novelty. So he played straight. That's true. I stuck to the melodic line. You know what I was playing. Well, did you know what the Negro followed me with playing? It says he built it on chords. That's a lie. He built it on my tunes in the marches that I played around the streets that they played in the carnival parades. Because no Negro played the carnival parades. They may have played in marching bands, and I don't remember them in my early times playing in marching bands. And as far as the funerals, they never played them in my days. That's all only lately since the jazz club to give credence that these people buried them by... This marching business, a march, a burial, came in with the military first. Then come the societies. Then come the different other people like the volunteer fire department, which I played. I played four different funerals for them. Jacqueline had the job, but I was the leader of the job. And they'd have a few men that read. I was a faker. But once I heard a tune, I could play it. And if I didn't play it, what I played never went against what the other man was playing. Because it would be either a harmony note or another note that would coincide with what he was playing. And many of the tunes, like Flea is a Bird, this fellow Papi, that this is one of the men that had bands out on the road too. He would be the cornet player. And he played a melody, and I'd play along with him. He had rock on baritone. He was a reader. Old man Alexander on helicon tuba. He was in a timing school in the old country. Today, they got him down to Kilbilly as one of the first jazz men. They got a picture of him in a great big thing down in Kilbilly as the first jazz. And this man played no jazz. But he did play with Jacqueline on his funerals. And did he play by ear at all? Oh yeah, he could fake. Any good reader could fake just some bass parts, common chords. Look, if you were a musician, what does it take to fake a common chord? All the chords in the common tunes are almost all identical. They had no accidentals in them. And if you knew one tune, it had to change after so many bars. The chord change would go from, say for instance, you were in, say take the key of B flat. Then you'd go to F7. From F7, you'd go back to B flat. Then B flat 7. Then the top chord, E flat. Then you'd come back to the major chord. Who the devil couldn't play that? You wouldn't have to be a note reader to play that. Faker could play it. Note reader could play it along with a fake band. All they had to do was play. And those men played by music, and they could not play anything jazz. They played ragtime. Like they were playing off their music, and it was a different rhythm. Ragtime had a jumping rhythm. And jazz was a smooth rhythm. It may be a cousin to it, but it has no part of it. In other words, when you play jazz, you're smoothed. You can write ragtime, but you couldn't write jazz. When we had our pieces to be taken down in notation, Miss Claim couldn't put them down. And the men in New York couldn't put them down the way they were. But today, they have signs to put over them. And the men, they know what they are. Why did they know what they are? Because they heard them on the record made by someone before them. I see a realist being around me.

segments.chapter: London and return to New York
segments.title: Savoy Peace Ball in London, Marble Arch, and buying out Emil Christian
segments.summary: La Rocca recalls the band playing the Peace Victory Ball at the Savoy before royalty and the reception for the NC4 flyers, then returning to America and buying out Emil Christian's share so he could go back to England.

segments.chapter: London and return to New York
segments.title: Emil Christian's letter and why New Orleans men could not play the Dixieland rhythm
segments.summary: A 1920 letter from Christian asks for Dixieland-style players rather than New York men. La Rocca argues no New Orleans band had the original band's rhythm and says laws in 1921 forced the band off Broadway.

segments.chapter: London and return to New York
segments.title: Band personnel after returning from London
segments.summary: The interviewer asks who was in the band; La Rocca names Robertson on piano, Shields, Sbarbaro, Edwards and saxophonist Benny Kruger, who was versatile but not a jazz man.

segments.chapter: New York dance halls and one-nighters
segments.title: Gilda Gray and the shimmy at the Follies Bergere
segments.summary: Gilda Gray danced the shimmy with the band for about two weeks as a showcase, put there by the owners, before landing a big part in the Ziegfeld Follies.

segments.chapter: New York dance halls and one-nighters
segments.title: Objections to the dance and La Rocca's crowd-rousing tricks
segments.summary: People said the music was sexual and ruined girls' morals. La Rocca describes sneaking off the stand while the crowd kept rhythm and imitating a woman's holler from his horn to whip the room up.

segments.chapter: New York dance halls and one-nighters
segments.title: One-night stands, guarantees, handling the money, and the Memphis Five
segments.summary: La Rocca describes touring one-nighters on guarantees plus percentages, counting the door, carrying cash in a money belt and splitting five ways. He then covers Robertson and Margie, replacing him with Signorelli, Shields leaving, and the Memphis Five.

segments.title: Working as an electrician and hearing the colored bands at the De Soto Hotel
segments.summary: Asked about raids, La Rocca says he was not allowed in the place but worked as an electrician for a construction company and heard the colored bands play at the De Soto Hotel.

segments.title: Robichaux and white bands left out of the history of Louisiana music
segments.summary: La Rocca says histories credit only Negro bands and ignore white bands, string bands, the Fourth of July and Bastille Day celebrations, German bands and French opera musicians, and he recalls working on the French opera stage.

segments.title: Counterpoint, New Orleans ragtime bands, Jack Laine's potato men, and Piron's music
segments.summary: La Rocca says his counterpoint came from opera, lists the Bohler, Detroit and Shimmer bands and Tom Brown, and ridicules Jack Laine's paraders. He says Piron sent him music including Sister Kate, which he arranged.

segments.title: Lytell and Signorelli's recording of Sister Kate
segments.summary: La Rocca says Lytell and Signorelli took his whole Sister Kate arrangement and recorded it, and that his correspondence with Piron predates Clarence Williams coming to New York.

segments.title: Clarence Williams, Buddy Bolden and Louis Armstrong's style
segments.summary: La Rocca argues Clarence Williams could not have heard Bolden play, given dates he cites, and says Armstrong's style came from the Original Dixieland Jazz Band records.

segments.title: Don Fowler's letter quoting Armstrong on the Dixieland records
segments.summary: The interviewer reads a 1958 letter quoting Armstrong's Satchmo, where he listened to the original band's Livery Stable Blues and Tiger Rag in 1918, and a note on the Louisiana Five.

segments.title: Joe Oliver, New Orleans historians, and the 1936 reorganization
segments.summary: La Rocca says Oliver and the Louisiana Five took from the band's records, attacks pro-Negro historians and Marshall Stearns, and says Tom Brown made untrue claims when the band was reorganized in 1936.

segments.chapter: Tom Brown's band and the first Dixieland claim
segments.title: Marshall Stearns's 1937 letter to La Rocca
segments.summary: The interviewer reads Stearns's January 1937 letter about the argument over colored musicians. La Rocca accuses Stearns of being pro-communist and says articles copied from him hurt a working man.

segments.chapter: Tom Brown's band and the first Dixieland claim
segments.title: Bill Lambert's letter on Brown's band and La Rocca's angry response
segments.summary: Lambert's 1936 letter recalls Brown's band in Chicago and Hoboken around 1915. La Rocca, calling Lambert Brown's drummer, denounces historians, defends his compositions and says Dixieland started name bands and arrangements.

segments.chapter: Tom Brown's band and the first Dixieland claim
segments.title: Brown's band lineup, Chicago failure, and New Orleans recruiting in Exchange Alley
segments.summary: La Rocca lists Brown's players, says they were part fakers and ragtime and made no success in Chicago, and describes bands recruited from Exchange Alley for circuses and road shows before Brown.

segments.chapter: Defending the music and its origins
segments.title: Edwards on trombone, borrowed chords, and the band's new rhythm
segments.summary: La Rocca praises Edwards as father of modern trombone, defends tunes built on common chord structures, says the band's rhythm was new, criticises modern players' stamina, and disputes that rhythm came from Africa.

segments.chapter: Defending the music and its origins
segments.title: Faking, funerals, parade bands, and ragtime versus jazz rhythm
segments.summary: La Rocca describes how fakers invented jazz licks, says Negro bands did not play carnival parades or funerals in his day, and distinguishes ragtime's jumping rhythm from jazz's smooth rhythm.
